content: In a controlled exposure chamber study, five male volunteers were exposed to monochlorobenzene at concentrations of either 12 ppm (55 mg/m³) or 60 ppm (276 mg/m³) for a duration of 7 hours. Pharmacokinetic models were employed to calculate the elimination curves of the major urinary metabolites. For the purposes of these calculations, the exposure was standardized to 1 ppm chlorobenzene, and it was assumed that the absorption rate of chlorobenzene in the lungs was 100%. Measurements of chlorobenzene in blood, and potentially in exhaled air, can be utilized for monitoring purposes. However, the most reliable biological exposure indicators for chlorobenzene in humans are the urinary concentrations of 4-chlorocatechol and p-chlorophenol. These metabolites are quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). One method involves treating urine samples with perchloric acid at 95°C, followed by extraction of the metabolites using diisopropyl ether. The ether fraction is then evaporated, and the residue is dissolved in a mixture of acetonitrile and water. An aliquot of this solution is separated on a column packed with, for example, Chrompack C18, using a mobile phase consisting of acetonitrile, water, and hexasulphonic acid. Recently, Ogata et al. described a modified procedure that eliminates the ether extraction step. In this revised protocol, urinary samples are treated with various enzymes, and the enzymatic hydrolysates are directly applied to an HPLC column for analysis. One of the earliest studies demonstrating a strong correlation between air concentrations of chlorobenzene and urinary concentrations of its metabolites was conducted by Yoshida et al. In this field study, chlorobenzene concentrations were measured in the air of two different chemical factories using personal air sampling devices. The study involved 11 subjects, with exposure times per shift ranging from 8 to 11 hours. Another field study conducted in Belgium involved 44 male workers in a plant producing diphenylmethane-4,4'-diisocyanate. This study confirmed the strong correlation between air concentrations of chlorobenzene and urinary levels of 4-chlorocatechol and 4-chlorophenol at the end of the work shift.
